FINDING_ID: ROUND16_F001  
SEVERITY: 0.89  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION: 0.84  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`DynamicManager.process_round()` can execute the adaptive-update path after `critical_failure` has already been determined, causing side effects after a logically terminal failure.** The method sets `critical_failure=True` from failure handling and `should_abort()`, but still proceeds to update convergence state, diminishing-returns state, and may emit normal progress events before terminalizing. More subtly, termination is decided only after those mutations, so a PM-fatal round is still treated as valid evidence for learning and stopping logic. This is deeper than “FAIL_CRITICAL doesn’t take precedence” at the FSM boundary: the entire orchestration pipeline violates fail-fast semantics and contaminates post-mortem state with data from a round that should have been rejected as operationally invalid. The fix is to short-circuit immediately after unrecoverable failure determination, before updating convergence, diminishing returns, or fingerprint state.

FINDING_ID: ROUND16_F002  
SEVERITY: 0.86  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION: 0.82  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`process_round()` has no consistency check that `responses`, `findings`, and `failure_handler.active_models` refer to the same participating set at the instant of processing, creating a race-like internal contradiction even in single-threaded use.** Failure handling may exclude models while iterating `responses`; later logic still processes the full `findings` list and records the resulting round as if all evidence were admissible. A model can therefore be excluded during the round yet still contribute findings to convergence and diminishing-returns metrics in that same call. This is distinct from generic “unknown/inactive model accepted” findings: the missed issue is the **intra-call temporal inconsistency** between failure adjudication and evidence acceptance. The manager needs a single validated round snapshot, or it must filter findings/responses to the surviving admissible set after failure classification.

FINDING_ID: ROUND16_F003  
SEVERITY: 0.83  
FLAW_CLASS: 1  
ABSTRACTION: 0.79  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`DynamicManager.get_allocation()` claims “Every active model gets work matched to its demonstrated capability,” but the implementation can legally return allocations that assign zero tasks to some active models with no signal to the caller.** `LoadBalancer.solve()` only enforces per-task coverage, not per-model utilization, and the greedy heuristic sorts by current load fraction. If tasks are few or large, some active models will remain idle despite the API contract asserting universal work assignment. This is not just a documentation nit: downstream orchestration may assume non-response from an active model is meaningful, when in fact that model may simply have had no assigned work. The missing invariant is an explicit representation of expected responders / idle models in the public API.

FINDING_ID: ROUND16_F004  
SEVERITY: 0.81  
FLAW_CLASS: 4  
ABSTRACTION: 0.77  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **The orchestration layer has no stable notion of “round identity” that spans allocation, dispatch-feasibility checks, responses, and results, so actions from different logical rounds can be interleaved without detection.** `get_allocation()` does not mint a round token, `check_dispatch_feasibility()` uses the current mutable FSM round, and `process_round()` accepts arbitrary caller data later. Because none of these APIs are bound together, a caller can compute an allocation for one state, dispatch partially, advance state elsewhere, then process stale responses against the new state. Prior findings noted missing allocation persistence and weak round-index validation, but the deeper missed flaw is the absence of an end-to-end protocol object tying decision, execution, and ingestion together. This makes correct external orchestration impossible to guarantee.

FINDING_ID: ROUND16_F005  
SEVERITY: 0.78  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION: 0.75  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`FailureHandler.detect_failure()` and `get_recovery()` are not side-effect isolated, so merely probing failure status mutates long-lived manager state.** Detection appends underperformance scores to `_perf_history`; recovery records failures and may exclude models. There is no read-only “classify” API. Any caller that re-evaluates a response, retries processing after an exception, or performs dry-run analysis will change future escalation behavior. Earlier findings covered duplicate evaluation poisoning underperformance history, but the broader missed issue is API design: classification and state transition are inseparable. The correct structure is a pure classification/planning phase followed by an explicit commit.

FINDING_ID: ROUND16_F006  
SEVERITY: 0.76  
FLAW_CLASS: 1  
ABSTRACTION: 0.73  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **The manager can silently lose observability for active models that produced successful but empty-finding responses, because there is no explicit “worked but found nothing” state anywhere in `RoundResult`.** Such models appear only indirectly via `responses`; they are absent from `findings`, contribute zero to fingerprint coverage/severity, and are not distinguished from models that were idle, omitted, or never assigned anything. This is a cross-cutting protocol flaw spanning allocation, failure handling, adaptive updates, and audit history. Without an explicit per-model outcome state, the system cannot reliably interpret silence, calibrate underperformance, or explain round behavior after the fact.

FINDING_ID: ROUND16_F007  
SEVERITY: 0.72  
FLAW_CLASS: 5  
ABSTRACTION: 0.71  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`ConvergenceDetector` and `DiminishingReturnsDetector` use incompatible abstractions of cumulative evidence in a way that can make stopping behavior path-dependent under equivalent semantic evidence.** Convergence clusters raw findings into equivalence classes on demand; diminishing returns consumes a flattened list of cumulative class members and then recomputes yield from member count and abstraction mean. Two semantically equivalent histories with different duplicate multiplicities can therefore have identical convergence behavior but different marginal-value trajectories. Prior findings identified duplicate inflation and novelty mismatches, but the deeper cross-subsystem problem is that the two detectors do not share a canonical representation of evidence. They should both operate over the same novelty/cumulative class basis.

FINDING_ID: ROUND16_F008  
SEVERITY: 0.69  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION: 0.68  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`DynamicManager` accepts mutable config by reference and propagates it into long-lived subsystems without any cache invalidation or reinitialization strategy, so mid-run config mutation can create split-brain behavior across components.** Some subsystems read config dynamically (`LoadBalancer`, `FailureHandler`), while others cache derived state keyed only by round index (`ConvergenceDetector`). If `tau_sim`, thresholds, or smoothing knobs are changed after construction, old cached classes and new decisions coexist under different semantics. This is broader than previously noted inert knobs or mutable vectors: the entire manager lacks a configuration immutability boundary.

FINDING_ID: ROUND16_F009  
SEVERITY: 0.64  
FLAW_CLASS: 4  
ABSTRACTION: 0.66  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **The event protocol is structurally lossy relative to manager behavior because it serializes complex state transitions into isolated flat events with no causal correlation ID.** A consumer cannot reliably tell which `CONVERGENCE_CHECK`, `STOP_CHECK`, failure events, and `ROUND_COMPLETE` notifications belong to the same processing attempt if `process_round()` is retried or partially fails. This is a deeper issue than wrong event types or missing recovery events: the event model itself cannot faithfully externalize the orchestration transaction. A round/attempt identifier is needed on every emitted event.

FINDING_ID: ROUND16_F010  
SEVERITY: 0.61  
FLAW_CLASS: 6  
ABSTRACTION: 0.63  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **The code treats BLIND, SYNTH, and iterative rounds as homogeneous economic units in diminishing-returns calculations, even though their semantics differ materially.** `process_round()` forwards a raw `round_cost` into the same detector regardless of phase, and `DiminishingReturnsDetector` has no notion of phase type. That means a high-cost SYNTH pass and a low-cost verification pass are smoothed together as if they were commensurate observations of the same process. This is not merely a tuning issue: it breaks the interpretation of marginal value over the lifecycle. The detector needs phase-aware normalization or the manager must exclude non-comparable phases from the same stopping series.

Definitive stance: there are still missed findings; the main new gaps are fail-fast contamination, missing round-identity binding, lack of pure classification APIs, and cross-subsystem semantic mismatches around evidence and observability.
